titre: Cuvier Proved Extinction by Comparing Elephant Jaws
accroche: In 1796, a young anatomist compares the bones of living and fossil elephants. He concludes that entire species have disappeared.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the 18th century, gigantic bones come out of the ground in Siberia and along the banks of the Ohio, and people wonder who they belonged to. Many suppose they come from beasts still alive in poorly explored regions of the world. To admit that an entire species could have disappeared is, at the time, anything but obvious: what it says about the Creation is debated, and every bone can always be filed under a known species.

## A Reading at the Institute

Georges Cuvier reads a paper on living and fossil elephants on January 21, 1796, at an ordinary session of the Institut national (the National Institute), then reads it again on April 4, 1796, at the Institute's first quarterly public session. An extract appears the same year in the *Magasin encyclopédique* (Encyclopedic Magazine). The full text, accompanied by five plates, is published in 1799 in the *Mémoires de l'Institut* (Memoirs of the Institute), although some sources give 1800.

## The Method: Comparing Bones, Not Guessing

Cuvier compares the skeletons, jaws and teeth of the Indian elephant, the African elephant, the Siberian “mammoth” and a fossil animal from North America, long called the “Ohio animal.” He first establishes that the two living elephants form two distinct species. He then shows that the mammoth is neither of them, and that the Ohio animal departs from them even more. According to National Geographic, which bases the comparison on the molars, he estimates that these fossils differ from elephants as much as, or even more than, a dog differs from a jackal or a hyena: such differences do not fit within variation inside a single species. He will name this animal the mastodon in 1806.

## An Extinction Without Evolution

The entry in the Garrison-Morton-Norman bibliography (historyofmedicine.com) presents this paper as the first scientific proof of the existence of extinct species. Cuvier nonetheless does not draw a theory of evolution from it: he will later explain the disappearances by successive catastrophes, and he will reject the ideas of transmutation of Lamarck and Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire. In his *Recherches sur les ossemens fossiles de quadrupèdes* (Research on the Fossil Bones of Quadrupeds, 1812), he will make it a system. What changes is the method: one no longer asks whether a bone resembles that of a known animal, one measures how its anatomy departs from it. Extinction is thus established by comparing bones, before anyone knows how to explain it.

repere.texte: Cuvier reads his paper on living and fossil elephants at the Institute on January 21, 1796, then on April 4, 1796; the full text, with five plates, appears in 1799. He distinguishes there the Indian elephant, the African elephant and the fossil mammoth, three separate species.

carte.punch: A species can disappear: in 1796, Cuvier demonstrates it with elephant bones.
carte.idee: The great fossil bones did not come from animals hidden somewhere. By comparing the skeletons of the Indian elephant, the African elephant and the mammoth, Cuvier shows in 1796 that the latter is a distinct species, and therefore extinct.

quiz.question: What does Cuvier's comparison of bones in 1796 show?
choix: That the mammoth is a breed of African elephant adapted to the cold
That the mammoth and the Ohio animal are species distinct from living elephants, and therefore extinct
That the great fossil bones come from animals still alive in unexplored regions
That extinct species slowly transform into present-day species
quiz.explication: Cuvier establishes that the mammoth and the Ohio animal differ from today's elephants as much as or more than a dog from a jackal, which places them in species of their own, now vanished. He does not draw from it a theory of the transformation of species: he rejects Lamarck's, and these are not animals still alive.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what anatomical basis does National Geographic place Cuvier's comparison between the elephants and the fossils?
choix: On the shape of the ears, the only soft part preserved
On the length of the forelegs
On the molars, whose differences exceed, in his view, those between a dog and a jackal or a hyena
On the color of the tooth enamel observed under a microscope
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to National Geographic, Cuvier bases the comparison on the molars, and judges the differences at least as great as those that separate a dog from a jackal or a hyena.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What theory does Cuvier develop to explain species disappearances, without seeing in them a gradual transformation?
choix: Natural selection, which he formulates before Darwin
Successive catastrophes, set out later in his Recherches sur les ossemens fossiles de quadrupèdes (1812)
The transmutation of species, which he takes over from Lamarck
The biblical flood as the sole and sufficient cause of all extinction
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cuvier explains the disappearances by successive catastrophes, developed in his Recherches of 1812, and he explicitly rejects the transmutation defended by Lamarck and Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What name does Cuvier give in 1806 to the fossil animal long called the “Ohio animal”?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cuvier names this animal the mastodon in 1806, after having distinguished it from the Siberian mammoth and from living elephants in his paper of 1796.
